Representative_Docs: ['DHS . ICEB-2 , Attention: Desk Officer for U.S. Immigration and , DHS I write in strong opposition against the proposed rule. Such a rule would place undue burden on international students who comprise a significant percentage of the national academic and research workforce. The timeframes proposed do not take into consideration the structures of graduate and postgraduate programs in the United States, which often exceed the proposed four-year limit. The proposed reduction in the F-1 grace period to 30-days does not account for the intense and intricate schedules academic and research workers often take on in their positions, and would result in increased disruptions to workplace productivity. Additionally, the proposed rules unduly target workers from the People’s Republic of China, who constitute a significant and vibrant percentage of the international workforce at US research institutions, which would likewise pose significant obstacles in the conducting of crucial research that benefits the national economy as well as the health and vibrancy of communities across the country. Furthermore, limiting the ability of international graduate students to change or transfer programs creates additional vulnerabilities to issues like harassment and bullying, while also preventing workers from adapting to an ever-changing industry. Transferring programs or institutions is often a last resort, most often due to uncontrollable circumstances, and must remain available, otherwise the U.S. risks losing valuable trained graduate students. Overall, the proposed rules would place undue burdens on international workers in American research and educational institutions, and would result in the deterioration of our work. I request that you take whatever steps are necessary to preserve the current duration of status rules and to strive to provide a more fair and efficient system for international students and scholars to study and work in the U.S.', 'As a PhD student who calls many international students friends, I urge DHS not to implement the proposed changes to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) and to maintain the current Duration of Status framework. The proposed policy changes will lead to a backlog of hundreds of thousands of extension requests that the current staff level at DHS cannot handle. This is unenforceable because it creates confusion for both college administrators and scholars and drives leading scientists away from American institutions. The detailed reasons are listed below: a. Virtually every doctoral program takes longer than 4 years. The Survey of from the National Science Foundation in 2024 estimates the average doctoral program takes 5.7 years, meaning that all doctoral international students would have to file an I-539 extension of stay form at least once. In 2023, there were 206,433 international students pursuing PhDs, or 15.3% of all international students at the time. b. Currently, the USCIS processing times tool estimates that an I-539 extension review for F, J, and M visas takes 3.5 months, unless applicants pay a premium price of $1,965. Representative_Docs: ['I have deep concern regarding the proposed rule to replace “duration of status” with a fixed four-year cap for F and J visas. This proposal would impose severe and unnecessary burdens on international students, universities, and ultimately the U.S. research ecosystem. Here is a breakdown of my concerns from the perspective of a PhD student. 1.PhD Program Length and The average duration of a PhD program in the United States is six years. Progress is highly dependent on research experiments, many of which are unpredictable and time-sensitive. For example, biomedical students may need to administer treatments to lab animals at specific stages of development, while those in fields such as quantum computing rely on fragile, high-maintenance equipment that can fail unexpectedly. The proposed four-year cap risks interrupting or even derailing critical experiments, delaying research progress, and wasting significant financial investment. 2. Administrative and Risk of Incompletion The requirement for repeated extensions would add layers of bureaucracy that jeopardize timely degree completion. Even a short delay in processing could push a student into unlawful status, despite their academic progress. This additional uncertainty will discourage talented international students from pursuing education in the United States, representing a direct loss to universities and the nation’s research competitiveness. 3. on Student Well-being and Mobility International students already face significant anxiety around visas. Many avoid traveling home during their studies out of fear that they may not be allowed to return and complete their degrees. This proposal would only deepen that insecurity. Additionally, the 30-day grace period after graduation is unreasonably short. It is barely enough time to pack belongings, let alone to transition to a job or postdoctoral position in the U.S. This effectively pushes graduates—who have already contributed years of research here—into taking their talents elsewhere. 4. of Talent to Other Countries The global academic environment is competitive. Countries such as Canada, the UK, and Germany are actively welcoming international students and researchers. By making the process more restrictive and stressful, the U.S. risks losing some of the brightest minds to other nations, weakening its own universities and research leadership. 5. Increased on Government Agencies With tens of thousands of F and J visa holders, requiring frequent extensions will generate overwhelming caseloads for USCIS. This will increase backlogs, delay processing, and strain government resources, undermining the very efficiency this rule claims to promote. 6. Restrictions on Major Changes PhD students often face unexpected circumstances—such as funding cuts, advisor changes, or evolving research interests—that necessitate switching fields or adjusting focus. Restricting flexibility in academic programs harms both students and institutions, and stifles innovation by forcing individuals to remain in unsuitable or unproductive academic tracks. In conclusion: The proposed changes create needless obstacles for international students, jeopardize research progress, and damage the long-term competitiveness of U.S. higher education. International students already bring substantial tuition revenue, innovation, and cultural diversity. Imposing rigid timelines, burdensome extensions, and an unreasonably short grace period risks driving this vital community away. I strongly urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve the current system of duration of status, which allows students to complete their studies without unnecessary disruption, while still ensuring compliance with immigration rules.', 'No.: ICEB-2 Comment Opposing Proposed on Duration of Status (D/S) for F-1 Students To Whom It May Concern: I am submitting this comment regarding the Notice of Proposed making on the elimination of Duration of Status (D/S) for F-1 students. I strongly oppose this change for the reasons outlined below. 1. to Academic and The proposed rule would impose arbitrary visa expiration dates, creating uncertainty that disrupts academic planning. Graduate and doctoral research often spans multiple years, and projects in STEM fields (Computer Science, Engineering, , etc.) require uninterrupted focus. For example, NSF reports that over 50% of graduate students in U.S. STEM fields are international students, many of whom are involved in multi-year federally funded projects. Introducing rigid visa limits would force students to constantly re-apply for status, diverting attention away from research and increasing the risk of losing highly skilled contributors mid-project. 2. and Innovation Impact International students are vital contributors to the U.S. economy and workforce. According to NAFSA (Association of International Educators), international students and their families contributed $40.1 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 368,000 jobs in the 2022–2023 academic year. Many students, particularly in STEM, transition to Optional Practical Training (OPT) and later to the U.S. workforce, filling critical shortages in fields like software engineering, AI, and cybersecurity. Restricting D/S would reduce this pipeline of skilled workers and harm U.S. competitiveness. 3. Negative Impact on U.S. Competitiveness Other countries are actively strengthening their ability to attract global talent: Canada offers international students multi-year study permits tied to program length, and post-graduation work permits without added uncertainty. The UK reintroduced the Graduate Route, granting international students two to three years of post-study work authorization. If the U.S. adopts restrictive D/S policies, it will lose its position as the top destination for global talent, especially in STEM, where competition is already fierce. 4. Existing is The SEVIS system requires schools to report student enrollment status, and U.S. consulates and USCIS have extensive authority to enforce compliance. Adding arbitrary visa end dates creates redundancy and administrative burden without improving oversight or security. Institutions already dedicate significant resources to ensuring students remain in status. This rule would shift focus away from education toward bureaucratic compliance, straining both universities and DHS without tangible benefits. 5. Unintended Consequences Mental Health and : Constant fear of status expiration would harm student well-being, especially given the rising rates of stress and anxiety among international students documented in recent surveys. Disproportionate Burden on Developing Countries: Students from countries with fewer U.S. consular posts may face extreme hardship renewing visas, leading to inequities. Risk of Talent Flight: Talented students may opt for other countries that provide stable, predictable immigration pathways. 6. Personal Perspective as a STEM OPT Participant I am currently on STEM OPT, having completed my degree in Computer Science in the United States. I am now applying the skills and knowledge I gained in U.S. universities to my full-time work, directly contributing to America’s technology industry and economy. The proposed change to eliminate D/S would not only undermine students still in school but also jeopardize the pathway for graduates like me who transition from F-1 to OPT and STEM OPT. My ability to work in the U.S., continue advancing research, and support critical innovation in software engineering depends on a stable and predictable immigration system. I came to the United States because it has been the global leader in higher education and technology. If stability and clarity are replaced with uncertainty and restrictions, future students and graduates may look to Canada, the UK, or other countries instead, weakening America’s role as a global innovation hub. Recommendation For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and maintain the current Duration of Status framework. The D/S system has successfully supported U.S. higher education, economic growth, and global leadership in innovation for decades. Eliminating it would create unnecessary uncertainty, reduce the attractiveness of U.S. institutions, and harm the long-term national interest. Respectfully submitted.', 'I strongly oppose the proposed rule to establish a fixed time period of admission and an extension of stay procedure for foreign students in the United States. While I understand the intent to standardize the admission process, this rule would create unnecessary hardship for international students, universities, and the U.S. higher education system. 1. Unnecessary Burden on Students and International students often pursue degree programs with varied timelines—such as doctoral programs, which are highly individualized and may extend beyond four years. A fixed admission period would force students to constantly apply for extensions, creating additional paperwork and financial strain, while also adding administrative burdens on universities and the Department of Homeland Security. 2. Negative Impact on U.S. Competitiveness The United States has long been a global leader in higher education by attracting the most talented students from around the world. Restricting admissions to a fixed period would make the U.S. less competitive compared to other countries (e.g., Canada, the UK, Australia) that provide more flexibility. This could discourage talented students from choosing U.S. institutions, reducing the country’s ability to maintain leadership in research, innovation, and global collaboration. 3. Disruption of Academic and Academic programs—especially in STEM and research-intensive fields—do not always follow rigid timelines. International students contribute significantly to federally funded research, community engagement, and teaching. Interruptions due to arbitrary admission deadlines would disrupt research continuity, delay graduation, and harm both the students and the institutions relying on their contributions. 4. Economic Harm to the United States International students are a vital part of the U.S. economy, contributing billions of dollars annually through tuition, housing, and living expenses. They also create jobs, enrich local communities, and support industries beyond higher education. Imposing rigid limits on their time of stay would reduce enrollment, shrink revenue for universities, and negatively impact the broader economy. 5. and Fairness Concerns The proposed rule risks disproportionately impacting students from certain countries, particularly those facing longer processing times or political restrictions. A case-by-case “extension” approach would create uncertainty and anxiety, leaving students unsure if they will be able to complete their studies or continue contributing to U.S. academia. 6. Alternative Solutions Already Exist Universities already report to SEVIS (Student and Information System) and have strict compliance requirements. These tools adequately ensure that students are maintaining lawful status without imposing additional, arbitrary limits on admission periods. Strengthening existing mechanisms is a more effective solution than adding new restrictions. Conclusion In summary, the proposed rule would harm international students, weaken U.S. institutions, damage the U.S. economy, and diminish the country’s global standing in higher education and research. I strongly urge you to reconsider and withdraw this proposal. A more flexible, student- and institution-friendly approach would better serve the goals of national security while maintaining the United States as a world leader in education, research, and innovation.']

Representative_Docs: ['I am writing to express serious concerns about the proposed rule’s restrictions on F-1 students’ ability to pursue programs at the same or lower educational levels. While I understand DHS’s goal to maintain program integrity, some provisions in this rule will cause significant harm to legitimate students and should be reconsidered. The Problem with Educational Level Restrictions The proposed rule states that F-1 students who complete a program cannot pursue another program at the same educational level or lower. This means students cannot pursue a second master’s degree, even in completely different fields. This restriction is too broad and will hurt many legitimate students. Real-World Impact on Students Many professionals need different types of graduate education for career advancement. For example: • An engineer with an MS in Engineering who wants to pursue an MBA for business skills • A computer science graduate who needs a master’s in data science for specialization • Healthcare workers pursuing additional certifications or specialized master’s programs • Students whose career goals change after gaining work experience These are legitimate educational pursuits that help students become better contributors to the US economy, not attempts to abuse the system. MBA Programs Are Particularly Affected MBA programs are professional degrees that many students pursue as a second master’s after gaining work experience. The proposed rule would essentially ban international students from pursuing MBAs if they already have any master’s degree. This makes no sense because: • MBA programs are designed for working professionals who often already have graduate degrees • Business education is fundamentally different from technical or academic fields • Many US business schools specifically recruit students with diverse educational backgrounds Suggested Solutions Instead of a complete ban on same-level education, I recommend: 1. Allow 2-3 master’s degrees maximum: This would prevent indefinite program switching while allowing legitimate career development. 2. Create exceptions for professional programs: MBA, JD, MD, and other professional degrees should be treated differently from academic master’s degrees. 3. Focus on time limits: The 4-year maximum admission period already addresses concerns about indefinite stays. Additional educational level restrictions are unnecessary. 4. Case-by-case review: officers to evaluate whether a second program serves legitimate educational and career goals. Why This Matters International students contribute billions to the US economy and often stay to work in critical fields. Overly restrictive rules will: • talented students to other countries like Canada, UK, and Australia • Hurt US universities that depend on international student tuition • Reduce the pool of skilled workers available to US companies • Damage America’s reputation as a destination for higher education Conclusion I strongly urge DHS to revise or remove the educational level restrictions in this proposed rule. The current language is too broad and will harm legitimate students while doing little to address actual fraud concerns. The existing time limits and oversight mechanisms are sufficient to maintain program integrity. Please consider allowing at least 2-3 master’s degrees and creating clear exceptions for professional programs like MBAs. This would strike a better balance between security concerns and the legitimate educational needs of international students.', 'This is an excerpt from the full comment. Please see the file attached for the full comment. I am writing in response to the proposed rule to establish a fixed time period of admission for F, J, and I nonimmigrants. While I appreciate DHS’s stated goal of ensuring program integrity and national security, I have significant concerns about the unintended consequences of this rule on international students, U.S. higher education institutions, and the nation’s long-standing role as a global leader in education. 1. Maintain Opportunities for Students Pursuing at the Same Educational Level The proposed restriction on international students who seek to enroll in another program at the same academic level (e.g., a second master’s degree) would severely disadvantage many students. In practice, numerous students pursue an additional degree at the same level to: - Pursue new career development opportunities and build new connections. For example, a student who completes a master’s in marketing may later pursue a master’s in business analytics to gain advanced quantitative skills that complement their prior training. This kind of academic progression helps them qualify for higher-level roles in strategy, product management, or analytics-driven marketing, while also expanding their professional networks and competitiveness in the labor market. - Transition to a different field or industry during rapid technological development. In other cases, students use a second master’s to pivot into a new career path altogether. For instance, someone with a master’s in media studies might later pursue a second master’s in digital communications or social media analytics to shift into technology-enabled marketing or content strategy. - Explore new academic and personal interests. Not every second degree is driven by career necessity; some graduates pursue another master’s program to broaden their intellectual horizons and pursue new passions. ’s programs provide the right length and depth for graduates to explore new interests in life, allowing international students to grow personally as well as professionally. - Avoid unfairly penalizing the majority for rare cases of abuse. While a few students may have historically enrolled in multiple programs without clear academic intent, such cases are rare. U.S. master’s degrees are prohibitively expensive for most international students to misuse without a genuine desire for further education. It is not reasonable to remove the opportunity for a second degree at the same educational level from all international students based on isolated abuses. To do so would punish the vast majority of law-abiding students who pursue additional programs for legitimate academic, professional, and personal advancement. - Even in rare situations where students remain enrolled longer, they are still paying tuition, supporting U.S. educational institutions, and contributing to the local economy. There is nothing inherently negative about this — international students’ financial contributions allow universities to grow, fund research, and create jobs. 2. Longer Admission Periods based on program duration The proposed four-year maximum admission period is not realistic for doctoral education. PhD programs in the United States routinely require five to seven years of study to complete, due to coursework, qualifying exams, research, and dissertation requirements. Forcing students to apply for extensions mid-program will: * Increase the administrative burden on USCIS and schools; * Disrupt students’ research and academic progress; * Create uncertainty for talented individuals who often commit most of their 20s to academic training. I urge DHS to allow program-based admission periods that reflect the documented normal duration of doctoral programs, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all four-year cap. 3. Clarify for Students with The proposed rule risks penalizing students who travel internationally while a timely Extension of Stay (EOS) or Employment Authorization Document (EAD) application is pending. The rule should provide clear and uniform guidance to ensure students do not inadvertently abandon valid applications by departing the country for legitimate reasons such as family emergencies, academic research, or conferences. This issue is especially critical for PhD students, who frequently need to travel abroad to present their research at international academic conferences, collaborate with colleagues, or conduct fieldwork. Such activities are essential components of doctoral training and benefit U.S. universities directly. Without clear rules, these students may be forced to choose between advancing their academic careers and maintaining their lawful status.', '1. The proposed regulation states: “An alien who has completed a program as an F-1 nonimmigrant at one educational level may not maintain, be admitted, or otherwise be provided F-1 status through a program at the same educational level or a lower educational level.” In practice, this would mean that a student who has completed one master’s degree (or a PhD) would have zero opportunity to pursue another master’s program in the United States, even in a different discipline. Previously, there was no limit on how many times a student could enroll at the same level. Moving from “unlimited chances” to “zero additional chances” is too drastic. A middle-ground policy — permitting one additional program at the same level — would address the government’s concern about serial enrollments while preserving legitimate opportunities. 2. Analysis: 2.1. Balanced solution: DHS’s concern about repeated, same-level enrollment is understandable, but a blanket ban is unnecessarily restrictive. A reasonable cap of two programs per level would deter abuse without unfairly penalizing students who pursue legitimate second degrees, such as an MBA after a PhD in science or engineering. 2.2. Legitimate career pathways: Many highly trained individuals pursue a second master’s in a different discipline — for example, scientists or engineers who earn an MBA to move into leadership, management, or entrepreneurship. These are not duplicate studies but intentional career transitions that expand U.S. workforce capacity. 2.3. No evidence of abuse: Pursuing multiple master’s degrees is not an immigration violation. International students are lawfully admitted, pay tuition in full, and meet program requirements. Regardless of how many master’s degrees they pursue (within a reasonable cap), this remains a legal, personal educational decision. 2.4. Economic and institutional impact: International students contribute billions of dollars annually to U.S. universities and local economies. MBA and other professional programs in particular rely heavily on international enrollment. By moving to a zero-tolerance rule, DHS risks significant financial losses for universities and diminished U.S. competitiveness in attracting global talent. 2.5. Workforce consequences: Today’s workforce requires interdisciplinary training. A clinician who pursues a public health degree or a PhD scientist who adds an MBA often goes on to lead companies or influence health policy. Removing this pathway harms innovation and reduces U.S. leadership in critical fields. 3. Recommendations I respectfully urge DHS to: 1) Adopt a reasonable cap: Allow F-1 students to enroll in up to two programs at the same educational level (rather than only one), to balance DHS’s concerns with students’ legitimate academic and professional needs. 2) second master’s programs in distinct disciplines (e.g., MBA after PhD or MSc), recognizing that these are career transitions, not duplications. 3) Recognize the economic contributions of international students who pay full tuition and strengthen U.S. higher education. 4) Affirm academic choice and freedom: Students in lawful status who meet all academic and financial obligations should not be barred from pursuing additional education. 5) Consider certification by institutions: Rather than banning second master’s programs, allow schools to certify that the program is academically distinct or professionally justified. 4. Conclusion In summary, moving from unlimited enrollment at the same level to zero additional opportunities is too extreme. A fairer and more balanced approach is to allow up to two programs at the same educational level, particularly when the second degree is in a different discipline that supports career advancement (such as an MBA). International students pursuing such paths are not abusing the system — they are paying tuition, following the law, and contributing greatly to U.S. higher education and the economy. I urge DHS to reconsider the proposed restriction and adopt a more measured solution that prevents misuse while preserving legitimate academic and professional opportunities.']

Name: 3_talent_rule_global_global talent
Representative_Docs: ['I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule eliminating duration of status (D/S) for F, J, and I nonimmigrants as a global talent strategy consultant who has advised governments on competitive immigration policies for over fifteen years. The proposed rule fundamentally misunderstands how talent mobility functions in today\'s interconnected economy. While DHS frames this as an immigration enforcement measure, it is effectively a unilateral economic disarmament that will accelerate the ongoing global talent redistribution away from the United States. Our competitor nations are already implementing aggressive talent attraction strategies—Canada\'s Start-up Visa Program, Singapore\'s Tech.Pass initiative, and the UAE\'s Golden Visa system—all designed to capture the mobile global talent pool that has traditionally flowed to America. The four-year fixed timeline creates what economists call "planning horizon distortion," where uncertainty about future status forces suboptimal decision-making. International students will increasingly choose programs based on immigration timelines rather than academic merit, leading to brain drain in precisely the sectors where America needs sustained leadership: artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and biotechnology. More critically, this policy signals to global talent markets that the United States views highly skilled immigration as a burden to be managed rather than a strategic asset to be cultivated. From a systems perspective, the proposed rule will create cascading inefficiencies throughout the talent pipeline. Universities will bear increased administrative costs, students will divert intellectual energy toward visa compliance, and employers will face greater uncertainty when planning multi-year projects. The net effect is a reduction in what development economists term "talent retention efficiency"—the percentage of trained individuals who remain productive within the system that invested in their development. Rather than implementing these counterproductive restrictions, DHS should adopt a risk-stratified approach that maintains D/S while enhancing monitoring capabilities. Specifically, I recommend implementing automated compliance scoring through expanded SEVIS data analytics, creating fast-track pathways for graduates from high-performing institutions, and establishing reciprocal talent mobility agreements with allied nations to maintain America\'s position in global talent networks. The proposed rule represents a strategic miscalculation that will diminish American economic competitiveness for decades. In an era of intensifying global competition for human capital, policies that increase friction for high-skilled talent are not just ineffective—they are economically destructive.', "I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed elimination of Duration of Status (D/S) for F, J, and I nonimmigrants as a global talent strategy consultant who has advised governments on competitive immigration frameworks for over two decades. This proposal fundamentally misunderstands the global talent marketplace and positions the United States for catastrophic strategic disadvantage. While DHS frames this as an administrative enhancement, the rule represents a profound departure from evidence-based talent retention policies that have proven successful internationally. The proposed four-year cap directly contradicts established research timelines in critical sectors. National Science Foundation data shows that median time-to-degree for STEM doctoral programs ranges from 5.8 to 7.2 years, with engineering and physical sciences averaging 6.4 years. Forcing mid-program extensions creates artificial disruption points that competing nations deliberately avoid. 's Post-Graduation Work Permit provides up to three years of post-study work authorization without arbitrary mid-program interruptions, while Australia's recent visa reforms extend stay periods to four years specifically to attract talent the U.S. risks losing. Most critically, this rule ignores the compound effect of talent networks. My analysis of patent filings and startup formation data reveals that international students who remain in the U.S. generate an average of $1.3 million in additional economic value through collaborative innovation networks over their first decade post-graduation. The proposed uncertainty disrupts these network formation processes, with cascading effects on U.S. innovation capacity that extend far beyond individual visa holders. The administrative burden analysis severely underestimates system-wide costs. Based on comparable policy implementations in other jurisdictions, actual processing costs typically exceed initial projections by 40-60%, while processing times create market uncertainty that deters top-tier applicants before they even apply. Rather than this disruptive overhaul, DHS should implement targeted reforms: establish risk-based monitoring using artificial intelligence to identify genuine compliance concerns, create fast-track extension processes for students in good standing, and develop bilateral agreements with key source countries for streamlined processing. These approaches address legitimate oversight concerns while preserving America's competitive position in the global talent market. The United States built its innovation leadership through strategic openness to global talent. This rule abandons that winning formula precisely when international competition for the world's brightest minds intensifies. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue evidence-based alternatives that strengthen both security and competitiveness.", 'I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule eliminating Duration of Status (D/S) for F, J, and I nonimmigrants. As a global talent strategy consultant who has advised governments and multinational corporations on human capital competitiveness, I am alarmed by the strategic miscalculation this proposal represents in the context of intensifying international competition for high-skilled talent. The proposed rule fundamentally misunderstands the modern global talent ecosystem. Today\'s most valuable human capital—particularly in emerging technologies, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing—is increasingly mobile and selective about destination countries. The OECD\'s recent shows that policy predictability and administrative efficiency are now primary factors in talent location decisions, often outweighing traditional considerations like salary or research funding. By introducing bureaucratic friction precisely where competitors are eliminating it, this rule positions the United States to lose ground in what McKinsey Global Institute terms the "talent wars" of the 2020s. Particularly concerning is the timing relative to competitor nations\' policy trajectories. \'s recent expansion of post-graduation work permits to six years for certain programs, the UK\'s restoration of post-study work visas, and Australia\'s streamlined skilled migration pathways represent coordinated efforts to capture talent the U.S. has traditionally attracted. Germany\'s new Opportunity and France\'s " " initiatives specifically target international students completing STEM programs. This proposed rule essentially provides these competitors with a significant policy advantage at no cost to themselves. The economic implications extend beyond direct student spending. PwC\'s 2023 analysis of innovation ecosystems demonstrates that early-career international talent serves as a critical bridge for technology transfer, cross-border investment, and market expansion. These individuals become the conduits through which U.S. innovations reach global markets and international capital flows back to U.S. institutions. Disrupting their pathways through administrative uncertainty creates downstream effects on venture capital availability, research commercialization, and export competitiveness that may not manifest for several years but will be difficult to reverse. Rather than implementing this disruptive change, DHS should consider establishing a risk-stratified monitoring system that maintains D/S for students in designated high-priority fields while enhancing oversight mechanisms. Additionally, creating fast-track extension processes for students demonstrating strong academic performance would address security concerns while preserving competitive advantages. Such targeted approaches would demonstrate sophisticated policy design rather than broad-brush restrictions that signal retreat from global talent competition. The United States built its innovation leadership through strategic openness to international talent. This proposal represents a fundamental departure from that successful approach at precisely the moment when doubling down on talent attraction would better serve national interests.']

Name: 4_physicians_training_medical_care
Representative_Docs: ['I am the Chief at my hospital in Brooklyn, New York, with oversight of 17 residency training programs with approximately 310 total residents. A number of our resident physicians are J-1 physicians. Our hospital, and our patients, rely on these physicians as a significant component of our physician workforce. Limiting the duration of status for these physicians to 4 years would be highly problematic and terribly disruptive to our hospital. This would not only potentially put the training of these vital physicians at risk, but also the patients they take care of every day. Please note that these comments are on behalf of myself individually, and do not necessarily represent the viewpoint of my employer, hospital, or institution. I agree wholeheartedly with the concerns about this proposal as outlined by Intealth ( URL "Replacing ‘Duration of ’ with a fixed 4-year cap would remove critical assurances that international physicians can complete their training, creating uncertainty that could disrupt residency programs, compromise patient care, and destabilize learning environments across the country. • Primary care pathways, such as Internal Medicine followed by subspecialty training (e.g., geriatrics, cardiology), routinely require 4+ years post-residency, putting these essential fields, already facing shortages, at particular risk. • General Surgery requires 5 years—status would expire before program completion. • Neurology and Psychiatry are 4-year programs—any leave of absence or other delay could jeopardize status. J-1 physicians currently are: • Thoroughly pre-screened, credentialed, and vetted by ECFMG (a division of Intealth) before entering the U.S. • Subject to biannual performance evaluations throughout their training • Monitored continuously by federal sponsors and accredited residency programs • Required to meet all U.S. medical licensing standards and operate under strict institutional oversight J-1 physicians occupy a uniquely regulated space within the U.S. medical education system, subject to rigorous oversight, fixed training structures, and ongoing evaluation. These standards are unmatched by any other J-1 exchange visitor category. Why Limiting Duration of to Four Years Is Problematic: Removing Duration of for J-1 physicians, who are among the most highly vetted, closely supervised, and continuously evaluated professionals in the United States, would inject uncertainty, increase administrative burden, and jeopardize the continuity of their critical training and patient care. It would also create severe logistical barriers for physicians: • Requirement to travel abroad to extend visa status • Unpredictable USCIS processing timelines for extension-of-status filings These requirements are unworkable for physicians engaged in full-time, highly structured clinical training and for the U.S. hospitals that depend on their continuous, reliable presence to provide essential patient care services. If Duration of cannot be preserved, the recommended pathway for physicians is to align status with the full length of their residency or fellowship program. This approach ensures continuity of training and prevents disruptions in patient care."', 'I am a Program Director for a physician fellowship training program, directly involved in training and supervising junior physicians. A majority of the applicants to our training program are physicians who hold J1 visas. These physicians are critical to our current and future physician workforce patient care mission. They contribute significantly to the United States healthcare workforce and any disruption of their ability to work will negatively and broadly impact healthcare services nationwide. J-1 physicians must be treated distinctly from other exchange visitor categories. The current D/S system has worked effectively for more than 30 years, ensuring uninterrupted physician training and patient care. It should not be changed. A change to fixed admission periods for J1 physicians would: 1. patient care due to USCIS processing delays and uncertainty. 2. continuity of training by making routine educational adjustments (remediation, parental/medical leave) subject to immigration adjudication. 3. Add significant administrative and financial burden for trainees and teaching hospitals. 4. Duplicate oversight, even though J-1 physicians are already highly vetted, accredited, and monitored through ECFMG, SEVIS, and ACGME standards.', 'Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule. I am a physician who leads residency and fellowship training programs at a health system with a substantial number of J-1 exchange physicians. My comments are based on my experiences as a leader in graduate medical education for 15 years supervising and training J-1 physicians, review of the medical literature, discussions with colleagues, and communication with and from standard-bearing organizations such as ECFMG and Intealth. More than 15,000 J-1 physicians are training in residency programs across the country; 3 out of 4 J-1 residents are in a primary care specialty (Internal Medicine, or Pediatrics), according to the ECFMG, with greater concentrations in hospitals and communities experiencing shortages. It is essential to emphasize that physicians are materially different from many other J-1 exchange visitor categories. Physicians’ training occurs in structured, accredited, and heavily monitored programs (ACGME-accredited residencies and fellowships or non-standard training programs). These programs include robust oversight, documentation, and institutional accountability, the very elements DHS has said it seeks to ensure. Those protections mean physicians already meet heightened standards of supervision and reporting, and that a one-size-fits-all approach would overlook these differences. The proposed mechanics of this change, including fixed admission periods, a four-year cap in many cases, and a requirement to apply to USCIS for extensions, create specific, concrete risks for physician training and patient care: 1. Training interruptions and delays. Today, Intealth and ECFMG sponsorship renewals maintain continuous status while programs continue. Under the proposed rule, trainees requiring more time would need USCIS adjudication. Given known USCIS processing backlogs and variability, adjudication could take months; that delay could force program interruptions or premature exits from training. 2.Potential loss of flexibility for remediation and leaves. training often requires in-program adjustments (remediation, parental or medical leave, extended training time for clinical competence). Requiring USCIS filings for each extension converts routine educational adjustments into immigration adjudication events, adding uncertainty, delay, and risk to clinical training pathways. 3. Administrative and financial burden on trainees and institutions. Currently, Intealth’s sponsorship renewals extend status without requiring individual USCIS filings. Under the proposed rule, responsibility for these filings would fall to trainees. This additional cost, paperwork, and timing burden for physicians and their institutions increases the risk of approval delays for trainees and staffing gaps for programs. 4. Duplication of oversight without improving program integrity. J-1 physicians already train in ACGME-accredited programs (or recognized non-standard programs), under Intealth sponsorship with DS-2019 monitoring and institutional oversight. Adding a new USCIS extension requirement duplicates review without necessarily improving educational or immigration compliance. 5. Threats to continuity of patient care. J-1 physicians provide essential clinical services across specialties and geographies. Any disruption to their ability to remain in training (or uncertainty that prevents hospitals from staffing confidently) will undermine continuity of care, especially in hospitals and regions that rely on international physicians to meet patient needs. At a time when the United States faces ongoing physician workforce shortages, converting program continuity to adjudication risk is likely to have material, negative effects on patient care and on teaching hospitals’ operational planning. This is particularly problematic because the current system works. Physicians are carefully vetted prior as part of the ECFMG certification process, thoroughly screened as part of the visa application process, constantly supervised while in training, and monitored in the Student and Information System (SEVIS) throughout their stay in J-1 status. For J-1 resident and fellow physicians, the current system works and to eliminate duration of status approval is to duplicate work, add administrative burden and delays for both physicians and governmental personnel and increase inefficiencies while adding nothing substantial to the rigor of the current processes for monitoring and vetting these physicians who have chosen to serve the American people. Without these physicians, thousands of residency slots would go unfilled, exacerbating the current physician shortage and worsening the health of Americans everywhere. I urge DHS to forgo enacting this rule, or at least maintaning Duration of Status approval for J-1 physicians if it will be eliminated for other categories.']

Name: 6_journalists_press_foreign_freedom
Representative_Docs: ['I am writing to urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw its August 28, 2025 proposal to limit the duration of visas for foreign journalists in the United States. These changes would harm press freedom and American interests more broadly by introducing the following unnecessary barriers and serious risks: Excessive administrative burden and uncertainty: Requiring frequent renewals every few months would distract journalists from their core work, and create anxiety about whether the visas they rely on for their livelihood will be renewed. Chilling effect on press freedom: Continuous scrutiny by government officials on an individual exercising their constitutional right to free speech, especially with the life-altering consequences of denying a visa based on an officer’s broad discretion, could lead to self-censorship and severely inhibit the freedom of the press in the US. Potential abuse: The new visa restrictions will leave journalists wondering if their visas will be cancelled because a single bureaucrat disapproved of the content of their journalism. Diminishing the standing of the United States abroad: Billions of people around the world, speaking thousands of languages, rely daily on journalists who understand their culture, as well as the context in the US. The absence of this reporting will diminish the standing of the United States while empowering its potential adversaries to fill gaps in reporting. Empowering authoritarian censors abroad: Requiring a journalist to be a representative of a foreign media organization will disproportionately harm independent journalists from repressive countries like Iran, Venezuela, and Russia, who are likely to not have a formal relationship with media in the country and more likely to face repression if expelled from the US. Given these self-defeating and concerning consequences, I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to abandon this proposal. Preserving freedom of speech and of the press by allowing law-abiding journalists to tell America’s story to their global audience makes America stronger and helps us live up to our founding principles. Name: 8_energy_clean_renewable_renewable energy
Representative_Docs: ["As the Chief Engineer at a leading renewable energy firm, I am deeply concerned about the proposed policy changes that would limit the duration of international students' stays and restrict their ability to pursue second degrees at the same or lower level. These changes could significantly impede progress in the renewable energy sector and hinder efforts to combat climate change. International students have been at the forefront of research and innovation in renewable energy technologies. According to the National Science Foundation, a substantial portion of research in clean energy technologies has been conducted by international students and scholars. Their contributions have led to advancements in solar, wind, and battery storage technologies, driving the growth of the renewable energy industry. The proposed policy changes would disrupt long-term research projects and limit the ability of international students to gain interdisciplinary knowledge by pursuing additional degrees. This could slow the development of new technologies and delay the transition to a sustainable energy future. Moreover, the renewable energy sector is a significant driver of economic growth. The International Renewable Energy Agency estimates that the renewable energy industry employed over 12 million people globally in 2020. Limiting the influx of international talent could stifle job creation and economic growth in this vital sector. I strongly urge policymakers to reconsider these proposed changes and continue to support the contributions of international students to the renewable energy industry and the global effort to combat climate change.", 'I am the COO of a renewable energy company, and I am alarmed by the proposal to replace Duration of Status (D/S) with fixed visa durations and restrict international students from pursuing second degrees at the same or lower levels. The renewable energy sector is critical to U.S. economic growth and environmental goals, projected by the International Renewable Energy Agency to create over 40 million jobs globally by 2050. International students constitute roughly 35% of graduate enrollments in environmental and energy-related fields, per the National Science Foundation. These students contribute to innovation in solar, wind, and battery technologies, sectors vital to achieving climate targets. NAFSA reports that international students inject more than $43 billion into the U.S. economy annually. Limiting their duration of stay will disrupt ongoing multi-year research projects critical for technology commercialization. Additionally, banning second degrees restricts interdisciplinary training in energy systems, policy, and engineering. The Department of Energy estimates that clean energy jobs could grow 60% by 2030, but this growth depends on a skilled, diverse workforce. If visa restrictions reduce international enrollment by 20%, the sector could face a talent shortfall costing billions in lost investments and delayed innovations. For the sustainability of the U.S. economy and to meet clean energy goals, I strongly advocate rescinding these policies. The D/S system and flexible academic pathways have been integral to attracting the global talent needed to power the energy transition.', 'I serve as an Engineering Manager at a renewable energy company focusing on solar and wind power technologies. The policy to replace Duration of Status (D/S) with fixed visa timeframes, alongside prohibiting second-degree pursuits at the same or lower levels, would severely harm the U.S. education system, economy, and renewable energy industry. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) forecasts renewable energy to constitute nearly 50% of U.S. electricity generation by 2030, requiring a highly skilled workforce in engineering and environmental sciences. According to the American Council on Education (ACE), international students make up approximately 37% of graduate-level environmental engineering programs, contributing critical research in energy storage, grid integration, and carbon capture technologies. The Clean Energy highlights a looming talent gap, with an expected shortage of over 400,000 clean energy workers nationwide by 2030. This shortage threatens to delay U.S. renewable energy goals and impact climate commitments. From the education side, the Institute of International Education reports that international students contributed $45 billion to the U.S. economy and supported nearly 460,000 jobs during the 2021–2022 academic year. Restricting their ability to pursue extended studies will reduce enrollment and research output in universities, undermining innovation. Prohibiting second-degree pursuits prevents students from gaining interdisciplinary skills vital in renewable energy, where engineering expertise often needs to be complemented by business or environmental policy training. The Department of Energy estimates that lost innovation from talent shortages could delay clean energy adoption by up to 7 years, costing the economy billions and harming U.S. leadership. Given these data, this policy will cripple both academia and industry progress. I strongly advocate that the government rescind this policy immediately to maintain the robust talent pipeline necessary for the U.S. renewable energy sector and economic growth.']
